summary: Specifies version 3 of the RFC Editor Model. Policy definition becomes the joint responsibility of the RFC Series Working Group, which proposes policy, and the RFC Series Approval Board, which approves it. Policy implementation is mainly the job of the RFC Production Center. It obsoletes RFC 8728 and was later replaced by RFC 9920.

plainLanguage.summary: This document describes how the RFC Series is run. A working group proposes rules for the series, an approval board signs them off, and a production centre carries them out by editing and publishing documents. It also creates a new stream, the Editorial Stream, for rules about the series itself.

questions: who is responsible for the rfc series
what is the rfc editor model
what does the rfc production center do
subtitle: Who writes the rules for the RFC Series, who approves them, and who turns them into published documents.

tldr.problem: The RFC Series is produced by several groups, and earlier versions of the RFC Editor Model left it unclear who could set policy, who approved it and who carried it out.
tldr.mechanism: Version 3 splits the work into two tasks. Policy definition belongs to the RFC Series Working Group, which proposes, and the RFC Series Approval Board, which approves. Policy implementation belongs mainly to the RFC Production Center, overseen by the IETF LLC, with advice from the RFC Series Consulting Editor.
tldr.outcome: The document also creates a fifth RFC stream, the Editorial Stream, for rules that apply to the RFC Series as a whole. It has been replaced by RFC 9920.

facts.label: RSWG chairs
facts.value: 2, one appointed by the IESG and one by the IAB

facts.label: Approval threshold
facts.value: At least three voting members vote YES

today: RFC 9280 was an Informational document published in June 2022. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9920, which is the current version of the RFC Editor Model. It also updated RFC 7841, RFC 8729 and RFC 8730, and was in turn updated by RFC 9720.

sections.title: The RFC Series and Version 3 of the Model
sections.content:
The Request for Comments Series is the archival series dedicated to documenting Internet technical specifications, including general contributions from the Internet research and engineering community as well as standards documents. RFCs are available free of charge to anyone via the Internet, and they have been published continually since 1969.

RFCs are generated and approved by multiple document streams. The stream approving body for each stream is responsible for the content of that stream, while the RFC Editor function is responsible for the production and distribution of all RFCs. The four existing streams are described in RFC 8729, and this document adds a fifth, the Editorial Stream, for publication of policies governing the RFC Series as a whole.

Under version 3 of the model, various responsibilities of the RFC Editor function are performed alone or in combination by the RFC Series Working Group (RSWG), the RFC Series Approval Board (RSAB), the RFC Production Center (RPC), the RFC Series Consulting Editor (RSCE), and the IETF Administration Limited Liability Company (IETF LLC), which together constitute the RFC Editor function. The intent is sustainable maintenance and support of the RFC Series based on expert implementation, clear management and direction, and appropriate community input.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC Series is the archive of Internet technical specifications. Several groups share the work, and this document says which group does what.

sections.title: Two Tasks: Defining and Implementing Policy
sections.content:
The document divides the responsibilities for the RFC Series into two high-level tasks.

The first is policy definition governing the RFC Series as a whole, which is the joint responsibility of two entities. The RFC Series Working Group is an open working group, independent of the IETF, that generates policy proposals. The RFC Series Approval Board is an appointed body that approves such proposals for publication in the Editorial Stream. The RSAB includes representatives of the streams as well as an expert in technical publishing, the RFC Series Consulting Editor.

The second is policy implementation through publication of RFCs in all of the streams that form the RFC Series. This is primarily the responsibility of the RFC Production Center, as contractually overseen by the IETF LLC.

The core activities follow from that split. The RSWG proposes policies that govern the RFC Series as a whole, with input from the community, the RSAB and the RSCE. The RSAB either approves a proposal or returns it to the RSWG, which may make further changes or remove it from consideration. Approved proposals are published as RFCs in the Editorial Stream and thus define the policies to be followed by the RSWG, RSAB, RSCE and RPC. The RSCE gives expert advice to the RPC and the RSAB on how to implement established policies on an ongoing basis, which can include raising issues or initiating proposed policy changes within the RSWG. The RPC implements the policies defined by the Editorial Stream in its day-to-day editing and publication of RFCs from all of the streams. If implementation problems arise, the RPC brings them to the RSAB, which interprets the policies and provides interim guidance to the RPC while informing the RSWG of those interpretations.
sections.plainLanguage: One group writes the rules, another signs them off, and a third follows them day to day. When the third finds a rule that does not work, the second interprets it and the first changes it.

sections.title: How a Policy Proposal Becomes an RFC
sections.content:
Policies governing the RFC Series as a whole are defined through a high-level process. Proposals must be submitted to, adopted by and discussed within the RSWG. Proposals must pass a Last Call for comments in the working group and a community call for comments. Proposals must then be approved by the RSAB. Policies under the purview of the RSWG and RSAB might include document formats, processes for publication and dissemination of RFCs, and overall management of the RFC Series.

The workflow has fifteen steps. An individual generates a proposal as an Internet-Draft and asks the RSWG to adopt it. The RSWG may adopt it as a working group item if the chairs determine by rough consensus that there is sufficient interest. The RSWG discusses and develops it. When the chairs believe there may be rough consensus, they issue a Last Call for comments within the working group. After a comment period of suitable length, the chairs determine whether rough consensus exists and, if so, announce their determination and forward the document to the RSAB. The RSAB then issues a community call for comments and, in parallel, considers the proposal itself. If substantial comments come back, the RSAB may return the proposal to the RSWG for revision, and an additional community call may follow.

Once the RSWG chairs confirm that the concerns raised in the community calls have been addressed, the RSAB polls its members. The positions are YES, meaning the proposal should be approved, CONCERN, meaning the proposal raises substantial concerns that must be addressed, and RECUSE, meaning the person holding the position has a conflict of interest. A member holding a CONCERN position must explain the concern to the community in detail. There are three reasons a member may file a CONCERN: that the proposal is a serious problem for one or more of the individual streams, that it would cause serious harm to the overall RFC Series, or that the community calls show a lack of rough consensus to advance it.

A proposal without any CONCERN positions is approved. If CONCERN positions remain after a suitable period, a vote of the RSAB is taken and the proposal is approved if at least three voting members vote YES. If it is not approved it is returned to the RSWG, which can consider further changes. If it is approved, a notification is sent to the community and the document enters the queue for publication as an RFC within the Editorial Stream. Policies may take effect immediately upon approval by the RSAB and before publication of the relevant RFC, unless they are delayed while the IETF LLC resolves pending resource or contract issues.

A community call for comments is announced with a subject line beginning with Call for Comments, a summary of the proposal, a URL pointing to the Internet-Draft, instructions on how to comment and a deadline. A comment period will last not less than two weeks and should be longer if wide outreach is required, and comments are publicly archived on the RFC Editor website.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposal starts as an Internet-Draft, is discussed and agreed in the working group, goes out for public comment, and is then put to the approval board. A board member can raise a formal objection, and if three members approve the proposal it goes ahead.

sections.title: Policy Implementation and the Production Center
sections.content:
Publication of RFCs is handled by the RFC Production Center. The general roles and responsibilities of the RPC are defined by RFCs published in the Editorial Stream, by existing RFCs that apply to the RPC and have not yet been superseded, and by the requisite contracts. The RPC is advised by the RSCE and the RSAB and has a duty to consult with them in specific circumstances, such as disagreements between authors and the RPC. It is overseen by the IETF LLC to ensure that it performs in accordance with the contracts in place, and it shall regularly provide reports to the IETF LLC, the RSAB, the RSWG and the broader community.

The RPC's responsibilities include editing documents originating from all RFC streams to ensure they meet the editorial standards in the RFC Style Guide, creating and preserving records of edits, identifying where editorial changes might have technical impact, establishing the publication readiness of each document, assigning RFC numbers, publishing RFCs and providing online access to them, providing an online system for the submission and display of errata, maintaining the RFC Editor website, and ensuring the storage and preservation of records.

Where a disagreement arises between the authors of an RFC-to-be and the RPC, and an existing policy clearly applies, the parties handle it by direct consultation. If it is unclear whether a policy applies, or how to interpret one, they consult additional individuals or bodies. A conflict with a policy for a particular stream is handled by consulting the relevant stream approving body, while a conflict with a cross-stream policy is handled by consulting the RSAB.
sections.plainLanguage: The Production Center is the company that edits and publishes RFCs. It follows the rules, and when a rule does not settle a question it asks the approval board to interpret it.

sections.title: The Editorial Stream
sections.content:
The document creates the Editorial Stream as a separate space for publication of policies, procedures, guidelines, rules and related information regarding the RFC Series as a whole. The Editorial Stream shall be used only for that purpose; no other use of it is authorized, and no other streams are so authorized. This policy may be changed only by agreement of the IAB, the IESG and the IETF LLC.

All documents produced by the RSWG and approved by the RSAB shall be published as RFCs in the Editorial Stream with a status of Informational. The Editorial Stream is not authorized to publish RFCs that are Standards Track or Best Current Practice, since such RFCs are reserved for the IETF Stream. Notwithstanding the status of Informational, documents published in the Editorial Stream define policies for the RFC Series as a whole.

Section 7 of the document lists the properties of the RFC Series that have historically been regarded as important, and proposals that might have a detrimental effect on them should receive heightened scrutiny during RSWG discussion and RSAB review. Those properties are availability, meaning no restrictions on access or distribution for many decades; accessibility, meaning a format intended to be as accessible as possible to people with disabilities; language, meaning all documents published in English and published under terms that allow translation without asking permission; diversity, meaning many types of documents including standards, procedural and informational documents, thought experiments, research papers, histories, humor and even eulogies; quality, meaning review for subject matter quality and professional editing with the goal of documents that are clear, consistent and readable; stability, meaning that published documents are not changed; and longevity, meaning publication in a form intended to be comprehensible to humans for decades or longer.
sections.plainLanguage: The Editorial Stream is where rules about the RFC Series itself are published. They carry an Informational status, but they still bind everyone who works on the series.

sections.title: What Changed from Version 2
sections.content:
The processes and organizational models for publication of RFCs have changed significantly over the years. In 2009 RFC 5620 defined version 1 of the RFC Editor Model, and in 2012 RFC 6635 defined version 2, which was modified slightly in 2020 by RFC 8728. The community experienced several problems with versions 1 and 2, including a lack of transparency, a lack of avenues for community input into policy definition, and unclear lines of authority and responsibility.

To address these problems, in 2020 the IAB formed the RFC Editor Future Development Program to conduct a community discussion and consensus process for the further evolution of the model. This document is the result of that discussion.

Several responsibilities previously assigned to the RFC Editor function are now performed by the RSWG, RSAB, RPC, RSCE and IETF LLC, alone or in combination. The responsibilities of the RFC Series Editor as a person or role are now split or shared among those bodies, and references in existing documents to the RFC Series Editor can be taken as referring to the RFC Editor function rather than to the RSCE. In practice the RPC and RFC Publisher roles have been performed by the same entity, so this document drops the distinction between them. The RFC Series Oversight Committee is disbanded, and the RFC Series Advisory Group, which existed in version 1 and was already gone in version 2, is affirmed to be disbanded. The Editorial Stream is created in addition to the streams already described in RFC 8729.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier versions of the model left too much unclear about who had authority. Version 3 spreads that authority across five named bodies, drops two groups that no longer had a role, and adds the Editorial Stream.

viz.caption: THE FIVE BODIES THAT MAKE UP THE RFC EDITOR FUNCTION

items.title: RSWG
items.text: An open working group, independent of the IETF, that proposes policies for the RFC Series.

items.title: RSAB
items.text: An appointed body that approves those proposals and interprets policy when needed.

items.title: RPC
items.text: The RFC Production Center, which edits and publishes the RFCs of every stream.

items.title: RSCE
items.text: A senior technical publishing professional who advises the RSAB and the RPC.

items.title: IETF LLC
items.text: The IETF Administration LLC, which oversees the RPC under contract and funds the work.

viz.caption: THE HISTORICAL PROPERTIES THE RFC SERIES MUST KEEP

cells: No restrictions on access or distribution, for many decades.
A format intended to be as accessible as possible to people with disabilities.
All documents in English, published under terms that allow translation without asking permission.
Many kinds of document, from standards and research papers to humor and eulogies.
Review for subject matter quality and professional editing for clarity and readability.
Published in a form intended to stay comprehensible to humans for decades or longer.

viz.caption: THE PATH OF A POLICY PROPOSAL THROUGH THE MODEL

messages.label: INTERNET-DRAFT
messages.note: A proposal is submitted and adopted as a working group item.

messages.label: LAST CALL
messages.note: The working group reaches rough consensus and forwards the document.

messages.label: COMMUNITY CALL
messages.note: A public comment period of at least two weeks.

messages.label: BALLOT
messages.note: Approved without CONCERN positions, or by at least three YES votes.

messages.label: PUBLICATION
messages.note: The document enters the queue for publication as an RFC in the Editorial Stream.
